This work belongs to the Kubjikā school, the *paścimāmnāya*. It contains detailed accounts of the fundamental ritual procedures of this tradition. It is likely that this work was not composed in Nepal, where she is nowadays worshipped almost exclusively. The following reference to Koṅkaṇa—that is, the region around modern Goa—in a colophon suggests that it may have been composed there:
"Thus, in the *Sūtrasaṃgraha*, in the section concerning Śrī-Koṅkaṇa."
This is by no means impossible, as we know that much of the early history of this school is associated with that region of India.

Oṃ, homage to the feet of the Guru.
I bow to that supreme reality, which is self-luminous, augmented by the three folds of bliss,
sixfold in nature, vastly expansive, and moving within the body.

O Mother, you who wear a garland of colors, protect us!
Having visualized a triangle upon one's own seat, one should worship that which is to be worshipped above in the three corners as well as in the center.

Aiṃ: That power called Bhaga, which possesses the triple-path course, is three-eyed and of three kinds; Hrīṃ: her Śrī is Oḍḍiyāṇa, joined with the Supreme Kalā (Parakalā), situated in the center and brilliantly radiant. Śrī-tac-chrī: that which is named Jālandhara, its manifest abode, is indeed in the southern corner; Khphreṃ is in the left.
The venerable Pūrṇapīṭha, by which the universe is filled and the fear of bound souls is dispelled.
In front of her is Hsvaṃ, the glorious Kāmarūpa joined with Madanakalā, the abode of all siddhas, and Śauṃ;
it is entirely triangular, adorned by the kalās of Paramaśiva and a multitude of yogins.

In the center of the *phreṃ* is the divine liṅga, which bestows supreme bliss; it is in the form of a drop (*bindu*), the nature of *kha*, the syllable *klīṃ*, and its essential nature is eternal bliss (*nityānanda*). Above that is the churning, distinguished by six methods.

Glūṃ! O Vidyā, experience the pure enjoyment of all objects of sense; O Aiṃ, you who pervade everything thus, the Mother of maintenance and dissolution, the power of Rudra through her threefold divisions, [reside] on the forehead of the Tisra-pīṭha.

Residing there, she is the Goddess of gods, bestowing bliss upon those who consist of both Akula and Kula; she is autonomous (Svatantrā), the command (Ājñā) marked by *Bhruṃ*, the one bound by [the fetters], the remover of fear for bound souls (paśu), and the embodiment of the multitude of divine Siddhas.

I bow to the one known as Śrī Kubjikā, who is eternally moist, intensely red, the supreme power of bliss delighted by the *bhaga*, renowned, the earth (*kṣmā*) that fulfills these desires, and whose beautiful body is agitated with passion.
Thus ends the Śaktisūtra.
On the path of the Meru of the continuum, the lineage-sūtra deity is the exit;

The house is said to be Candrapura, and the division is Manthānabhairava;

Fame is found in the *ciñciṇī* tree, and accomplishment (*siddhi*) indeed in the ocean;

The Goddess has a body that is full and perfectly complete, is red in color, and possesses three eyes with squinting glances. She has a triple-folded neck, one face, and two arms; holding a skull-cup and a trident in her hands, she gazes downward and stands upon a green lotus.

Having bathed with royal honors out of a desire for the fruits of merit,

Extremely subtle, supremely radiant, and having the nature of a thread from the *ūrṇā* [the circle of hair between the eyebrows],

The Śiva-tīrtha is a divine stream of nectar; it is neither an ordinary bathing place nor a matter of ritual observance. No one shall ever cease to be a partaker of that great tīrtha.
Stainless and of a radiant form, the supreme power (parākalā) resides within the Suṣumnā;

I am that supreme, auspicious, higher knowledge (parā-vidyā), whose nature consists of the three aspects; O Rudra, know me as the Power (Śakti) who manifests as the threefold [syllable] *tryakṣarī*.
She is subtle, she is gross, and she is fierce; she is of three kinds.

I shall further explain the division of this mantra for the wise one at the door, O fair-faced one: there are five at the beginning and five *praṇavas* at the end.
The knowledge situated in their midst is restrained by means of the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra],

By the cessation of its *repha*, that *vāruṇī* digit [resides] therein;
through this knowledge of the instrument (*karaṇa-vidyā*), that full moon (*pūrṇimā*) is revealed.
One should propitiate the Vidyā residing therein; otherwise, she turns her face away.
O Blessed One, at the beginning of the state, Kaulinī becomes Prakṛti.
The head is the seed-syllable *mālinī*, the nectar in the heart-lotus,
the moon and sun, and the *visarga* at the two breasts, O Goddess worshipped with excellent offerings.
The sixfold Khecara is established in the center within the six seats:
Uḍḍiyāna, the one called Hasakāma, Kha, Pha, Kuṅkaṇa, and Pūrṇaka.
The letter *repha* is the Jālandhara seat where that Kaulinī dwells;
these three currents within the triangle constitute this sixfold *khecara*.
The seven sciences have her as their foundation, and she is the Kaulikī Self.
Just as clarified butter is within milk, as the moon is among the planets,
and as Takṣaka is among the serpents, so is this Śiva who moves through the sky.
There is no mantra equal to this, even by hundreds of millions of mantras;
by the mere recollection of it, the state of being free from disease arises.
The venerable name is Kubjikā-yoni, and the Vidyā is the tongue according to their differentiation;
with the nasalized vowels, it becomes the nose at the Maṇipūra and the aperture of the hand.
The two syllables *chāṃ* and *chīṃ* are for the eyes; *kini kini* is the deity.
O Śambhu, when one understands this blood of all limbs— the instruction on the mantra— according to the sequence of the division of its words, agitation arises.
O Śiva, those born into the family of Yoginīs with whom I am pleased obtain the transmission of the Krama, the Kaumāra, which is difficult to traverse.
This is our primordial nature: the fivefold upper realm of the universe (brahmāṇḍa), the fivefold divisions in the netherworld (pātāla), the three paths, and the triple-pathed hermitage.
O fair-faced one, this indeed is the introduction to the root mantra.
